Stiff person syndrome (SPS) is an autoimmune disorder with multiple clinical presentations, all characterized by generalized or focal muscular stiffness leading to abnormal postures and movements.

Patients with SPS usually present stiffness in the proximal muscles, superimposed painful spasms, hyperekplexia (exaggerated startle response), and an increase in serum anti-GAD antibodies (Balint et al. , 2018).
Finally, generalized stiffness and confusion suddenly appeared, leading to hospital admission.

After 3 weeks, slight stiffness and mild pyramidal signs were present in the right limbs, but absent in the left limbs and the third GA was acquired (T2). At this time, the patient was able to move, run, and jump freely, without any sensory complaints; he also regained self-autonomy in daily activities and there was a significant improvement in both mood and quality of life (global clinical impression – severity was = 5; global clinical impression – improvement was= 1); Therefore, the family was reassured and satisfied by the good outcome.
